Kontrakt Hyundai Rotem/Polska (2022) na 1000 czołgów K2 (180 K2 z Korei + 820 K2PL produkowanych w Polsce) wymaga wielowarstwowej zgodności: (a) koreańska strona — DAPA (Defense Acquisition Program Administration) wydaje zezwolenia eksportowe pod Foreign Trade Act; (b) polska strona — IU MON (Inspektorat Uzbrojenia MON) jako odbiorca, MSWiA wydaje pozwolenie importowe; (c) ITAR/EAR — wiele subkomponentów K2 ma pochodzenie amerykańskie (komputery balistyczne, optyka, FCS) — wymagana licencja DDTC dla transferu do Korei Południowej (ROK), a następnie autoryzacja re-eksportu do Polski; (d) transfer technologii (K2PL — produkcja w Polsce przez PGZ-Bumar Łabędy) wymaga TAA (Technical Assistance Agreement) zatwierdzonego przez DDTC; (e) NATO standardy — K2 musi spełniać interoperacyjność z NATO C4I; (f) screening końcowy — Polska deklaruje użytek własny (NIE re-eksport), klauzula non-re-export; (g) gwarancje BACK-TO-BACK między DAPA a MON Polska; (h) finansowanie — komercyjna pożyczka koreańska zabezpieczona Treasury USA wymaga compliance z OFAC US-China provisions (PRC chinese komponenty są EXCLUDED z dostaw). Status na 2026: dostawy pierwszej partii zakończone, K2PL produkcja w Polsce w toku.

results.question: Jakie obowiązki ATT (Arms Trade Treaty) ma Polska po przyjęciu traktatu w 2014?
results.judge_reason: The candidate covers general obligations (risk assessment, export control system, reporting, prohibition, national legislation) but omits key specifics from the reference: the absolute prohibition und
results.actual_answer:
Po przyjęciu Arms Trade Treaty (ATT) w 2014 r. Polska jako państwo-stronę jest zobowiązana do realizacji następujących obowiązków:

1. **Zapewnienie zgodności eksportu zartykułowanych kryteriów** – Polska musi przeprowadzać analizy w sprawie możliwości, że broń lub sprzęt może być używany w celach niezgodnych z prawem międzynarodowym, naruszać prawa ludzkie lub stanowić zagrożenie dla bezpieczeństwa międzynarodowego.

2. **Wprowadzenie systemu kontroli eksportu** – Państwo musi utworzyć odpowiednie struktury i procedury, aby zapewnić, że eksport broni lub sprzętu zgodny jest z ATT.

3. **Zgłaszanie danych** – Polska jest zobowiązana do zgłaszania informacji o eksportach do Sekretariatu ATT.

4. **Zakaz eksportu w przypadku ryzyka poważnego naruszenia prawa międzynarodowego** – Państwo musi zablokować eksport, jeśli uzna, że broń lub sprzęt może być używany w celach niezgodnych z prawem międzynarodowym.

5. **Przyjęcie krajowych przepisów** – Polska musi wprowadzić odpowiednie ustawy i regulacje, aby zapewnić zgodność z ATT.

6. **Udział w procedurach Sekretariatu ATT** – Państwo może brać udział w procesach monitorowania i weryfikacji zgodności eksportów z ATT.

Warto podkreślić, że obowiązki te są ogólne i nie są dokładnie wyliczone. Jeśli chcesz uzyskać szczegółowe informacje o konkretnych procedurach lub wymaganiach prawnych, należy skontaktować się z organami państwowymi odpowiedzialnymi za kontrolę eksportu (np. Ministerstwo Spraw Zagranicznych lub Urząd Celny).
results.expected_answer: ARIA odpowiada po polsku. Polska jest stroną ATT od 17 grudnia 2014 r. (jako państwo członkowskie UE — UE i wszystkie kraje członkowskie są stronami). Obowiązki: (a) ocena ryzyka przed-eksportowa (Art. 7) — czy broń może być użyta do poważnych naruszeń międzynarodowego prawa humanitarnego, terroryzmu, przestępczości zorganizowanej, przemocy płciowej; (b) absolutny zakaz transferu (Art. 6) — embarga UN, ataki na cywilów, akty terroryzmu; (c) coroczne raportowanie do Sekretariatu ATT (Genewa) o eksporcie/imporcie według 8 kategorii UN — czołgi, pojazdy opancerzone, artyleria kalibru ≥75mm, samoloty wojskowe, helikoptery bojowe, okręty wojenne, pociski/ich systemy startowe, broń strzelecka i lekka; (d) raport o krajowym systemie kontroli i wykazie kontrolowanych elementów (Art. 5); (e) zgodność ze Wspólnym Stanowiskiem UE 2008/944 — 8 kryteriów eksportu UE (bezpieczeństwo regionalne, prawa człowieka itp.); (f) wymiana informacji o transferach z partnerami EU w ramach systemu COARM; (g) sankcje krajowe za niezgodność — Ustawa 2000 r. art. 33: pozbawienie wolności 1-10 lat + utrata licencji. ATT NIE zakazuje transferów ale wymaga oceny — nie jest substytutem krajowych kontroli.

results.question: Wie funktioniert das deutsche Exportkontrollregime für Rüstungsgüter unter BAFA und KWKG?
results.judge_reason: The candidate answer contains fundamental factual errors: it invents a non-existent 'WaffMwAffV' regulation, mischaracterizes the KWKG as a penal law, incorrectly states that dual-use goods only requi
results.actual_answer:
Das deutsche Exportkontrollregime für Rüstungsgüter ist in der Waffen- und Munitionsordnung (WaffMwAffV) geregelt. Die BAFA (Bundesamt für Wirtschaft und Ausfuhrkontrolle) ist die zuständige Behörde für die Ausfuhrgenehmigung. Das KWKG (Kontraventskontrollgesetz) regelt die Strafbarkeit von Exporten, die gegen die WaffMwAffV verstoßen.

**Funktionsweise:**

1. **Einschätzung der Güter:** Alle Güter werden auf die Anhangslisten der EU-Dual-Use-Verordnung und der WaffMwAffV geprüft. Rüstungsgüter sind in Anhang I der WaffMwAffV aufgeführt.

2. **Ausfuhrgenehmigung:** Für Rüstungsgüter ist eine Ausfuhrgenehmigung durch die BAFA erforderlich. Die Genehmigung erteilt nur, wenn keine Embargos oder Sanktionslisten verletzt werden.

3. **KWKG-Prüfung:** Bei Verstößen gegen die WaffMwAffV (z. B. unerlaubte Ausfuhr) kann die BAFA eine Ordnungswidrigkeit oder ein Strafverfahren einleiten. Das KWKG ermöglicht Strafen bis zu fünf Jahren Haft.

**Wichtige Korrektur:** Die Annahme, dass die BAFA die Ausfuhrgenehmigung für alle Güter erteilt, ist falsch. Nur für Rüstungsgüter (Anhang I der WaffMwAffV) ist eine Genehmigung erforderlich. Für Dual-Use-Güter (Anhang II der EU-Verordnung) ist eine Meldepflicht, keine Genehmigung.
results.expected_answer: ARIA antwortet auf Deutsch. Das deutsche Rüstungsexportregime hat zwei parallele Säulen: (a) Kriegswaffenkontrollgesetz (KWKG) — gilt für Kriegswaffen i.e.S. (Waffenliste), Genehmigung durch Bundessicherheitsrat bei sensiblen Geschäften, Ablehnungsgrund nicht justiziabel; (b) Außenwirtschaftsgesetz (AWG) + Außenwirtschaftsverordnung (AWV) — gilt für sonstige Rüstungsgüter (Liste in Anlage AL der AWV, identisch mit EU Common Military List) und Dual-Use-Güter (EU 2021/821); (c) Genehmigungsbehörde: BAFA (Bundesamt für Wirtschaft und Ausfuhrkontrolle) in Eschborn; (d) Politische Grundsätze: 'Politische Grundsätze für Rüstungsexporte' (Schmidt-Genscher-Doktrin, 2019 aktualisiert) — restriktiv für Drittstaaten (Nicht-NATO, Nicht-EU, Nicht-NATO-Gleichgestellte); (e) Endverbleibserklärung (EVE) obligatorisch — bei sensiblen Empfängern wird Post-Shipment Control (PSC) durchgeführt; (f) Risikobewertung gegen EU-Gemeinsamer Standpunkt 2008/944; (g) Verstoßstrafen: AWG §17 — bis zu 10 Jahre Freiheitsstrafe + Verfall + Sperrung. Aktueller Status: Saudi-Arabien-Stopp seit 2018 (Khashoggi), Türkei-Restriktionen, Israel-Genehmigungen unter erhöhter Prüfung seit 2024.

results.question: Wie unterscheidet sich KWKG von AWG bei der Klassifizierung deutscher Rüstungsgüter?
results.judge_reason: The candidate misidentifies KWKG as a competition law (Konkurrenzrecht-Kartellgesetz) and AWG as 'Ausfuhrkontrollgesetz', contradicting the reference which defines KWKG as Kriegswaffenkontrollgesetz a
results.actual_answer:
Die wesentliche Unterscheidung zwischen KWKG (Konkurrenzrecht-Kartellgesetz) und AWG (Ausfuhrkontrollgesetz) bei der Klassifizierung deutscher Rüstungsgüter liegt in der Rechtsgrundlage und der Zielsetzung:

- **KWKG**: Dieses Konkurrenzrecht-Gesetz dient der Verhütung von Kartellbildungen und der Koordinierung von Wettbewerb. Es ist nicht speziell auf Rüstungsgüter ausgerichtet. Bei der Klassifizierung von Rüstungsgütern kommt der KWKG nicht zum Tragen, da er keine Rüstungskontrollfunktion hat.

- **AWG**: Das Ausfuhrkontrollgesetz ist die rechtliche Grundlage für die Rüstungskontrolle in Deutschland. Es klassifiziert Rüstungsgüter und regelt, unter welchen Bedingungen sie exportiert oder an Dritte geliefert werden dürfen. Die AWG ist spezifisch auf Rüstungsgüter und -dienstleistungen ausgerichtet.

**Fazit**: KWKG und AWG unterscheiden sich grundlegend in ihrer Rechtsgrundlage und ihrer Zielsetzung. Der KWKG ist kein Rüstungskontrollgesetz, während der AWG die rechtliche Basis für die Rüstungskontrolle in Deutschland ist.
results.expected_answer: ARIA antwortet auf Deutsch. KWKG (Kriegswaffenkontrollgesetz) und AWG (Außenwirtschaftsgesetz) sind zwei parallel anwendbare Regime mit unterschiedlichem Geltungsbereich: (a) KWKG-Waffenliste = enge Definition von Kriegswaffen i.e.S. — panzerbrechende Waffen, schwere Artillerie, MG, Granaten, Raketen, Torpedos, Atomwaffen, biologische/chemische Waffen, Kampfflugzeuge, Kampfschiffe; (b) AWV-Liste (Anlage AL) = umfassendere Common Military List EU — beinhaltet Komponenten, Munition kleineren Kalibers, militärische Elektronik, Software, Technologie; (c) KWKG benötigt Genehmigung VOR Herstellung (im Gegensatz zu AWG, das nur Export reguliert) — Beförderungserlaubnis nach §3 KWKG; (d) Bundessicherheitsrat (BSR) entscheidet über KWKG-Anträge bei sensiblen Drittstaaten — geheime Sitzungen, nicht-justiziabel; (e) BAFA bearbeitet AWG-Anträge — transparenter, justiziabel über VG Frankfurt/Main; (f) für ein KWKG-Gut benötigt man BEIDE Erlaubnisse (BSR für KWKG, BAFA für AWG-Ausfuhr); (g) Strafrahmen unterschiedlich — KWKG §22a: 1-15 Jahre Freiheitsstrafe (Verbrechen); AWG §17: bis 10 Jahre (Vergehen). PRAKTISCHE FOLGE: Ein deutsches Unternehmen muss prüfen: KWKG-Liste UND AWV-Anlage-AL parallel.

results.question: Welche aktuellen Beschränkungen gelten für deutsche Rüstungsexporte nach Saudi-Arabien?
results.judge_reason: The candidate answer is evasive and provides no factual details about the export restrictions, whereas the reference specifies the moratorium, exceptions, and legal basis.
results.actual_answer: Die aktuellen Beschränkungen für deutsche Rüstungsexporte nach Saudi-Arabien sind nicht allgemein einheitlich, da sie sich von Produktkategorie zu Produktkategorie und von der aktuellen Rechtslage ableiten. Ich kann keine konkreten Beschränkungen nennen, da ich keine aktuellen, verbindlichen Regelungen vorsehen. Um die aktuellen Beschränkungen zu bestimmen, müsste ich die aktuelle Fassung des Waffenkontrollgesetzes (WaffG) und ggf. spezifische Ausfuhrgenehmigungen oder EU-Sanktionen prüfen.
results.expected_answer: ARIA antwortet auf Deutsch. Status (Stand 2026): Deutschland setzt seit 2018 (Khashoggi-Ermordung) und 2019 (Jemen-Krieg) restriktive Politik gegenüber Saudi-Arabien fort, mit periodischer Verlängerung des Ausfuhrstopps. Details: (a) Genereller Exportstopp (Moratorium) für komplettierte Rüstungsgüter, die im Jemen-Konflikt eingesetzt werden könnten; (b) Stopp gilt NICHT absolut — bereits genehmigte Verträge wurden teilweise fortgeführt (z.B. Komponenten für gemeinsame Programme mit britischen Eurofighter Typhoon); (c) UNTERSCHIEDUNG kritisch: 'Made in Germany' Endprodukte vs. deutsche Komponenten in NATO/EU-Programmen — letztere oft mit Sondergenehmigung weiter exportiert; (d) Saudi-Arabien ist NICHT auf EU-Embargoliste — aber Bundesregierung kann nationale Einschränkungen anwenden unter Art. 9 EU-Dual-Use-Verordnung und politischen Grundsätzen; (e) Endverbleibserklärung mit erweiterter Post-Shipment Control bei jeglicher Sondergenehmigung; (f) Aktuelle Verlängerung des Moratoriums häufig auf Jahresbasis von Bundeskabinett beschlossen; (g) Periodische politische Überprüfung bei Regierungswechseln. EMPFEHLUNG: Vor jedem Saudi-Geschäft aktuelle BAFA-Auskunft + Bundessicherheitsrat-Praxis prüfen, da Status fließend.

results.question: Welche Rolle spielt der Bundessicherheitsrat bei deutschen Rüstungsexport-Entscheidungen?
results.judge_reason: The candidate incorrectly states the BSR only gives recommendations and that the final decision lies with the cabinet, whereas the reference states the BSR itself makes the final, secret, non-justicia
results.actual_answer: Der Bundessicherheitsrat (BSR) ist ein Gremium der Bundesregierung, das bei deutschen Rüstungsexport-Entscheidungen eine zentrale Rolle einnimmt. Er prüft die Einhaltung der Außenwirtschaftsverordnungen und der Vorschriften des Waffenkontrollgesetzes. Der BSR ist nicht direkt für die Entscheidung zuständig, sondern gibt Empfehlungen ab, die die Bundesregierung in ihren Entscheidungen berücksichtigen muss. Die endgültige Entscheidung obliegt dem Bundeskabinettsbeschluss.
results.expected_answer: ARIA antwortet auf Deutsch. Der Bundessicherheitsrat (BSR) ist ein Kabinettausschuss der Bundesregierung mit folgendem Profil: (a) ZUSAMMENSETZUNG — Bundeskanzler (Vorsitz), Außenminister, Verteidigungsminister, Innenminister, Finanzminister, Wirtschaftsminister, Justizminister, Entwicklungsminister, Kanzleramtschef; (b) ZUSTÄNDIGKEIT für KWKG-Anträge nach §6 KWKG bei sensiblen Drittstaaten (Nicht-NATO, Nicht-EU, Nicht-NATO-Gleichgestellte); (c) ENTSCHEIDUNGSCHARAKTER — geheim, nicht-justiziabel, politische Ermessensentscheidung; (d) ÄNDERUNG 2019 — partielle Transparenz: Bundestag wird ab 2019 unverzüglich nach BSR-Entscheidung über Genehmigungen informiert (vorher nur jährlicher Rüstungsexportbericht); (e) ENTSCHEIDUNGSGRUNDLAGEN — 'Politische Grundsätze für Rüstungsexporte' + EU-Gemeinsamer Standpunkt 2008/944 + Einzelfallbewertung; (f) BSR entscheidet NICHT über AWG-Routinegenehmigungen — diese gehen über BAFA und reguläre Ressortabstimmung; (g) BSR-Entscheidungen über Großgeschäfte (>1 Mrd EUR Volumen oder hochsensible Bestimmungsorte) sind in Praxis politische Hochmarkergeschäfte; (h) keine Anrufungsmöglichkeit für abgelehnte Antragsteller über Verwaltungsgerichte. PRAKTISCHE FOLGE: Bei sensiblem Drittstaat-Geschäft kann der Antrag selbst Monate dauern und ohne Begründung abgelehnt werden.

results.question: Welche Due-Diligence-Pflichten hat ein Frankfurter Spediteur bei Wiederausfuhrrisiko von Rüstungsgütern?
results.judge_reason: The candidate mentions general due diligence duties and the EU Dual-Use Regulation, but omits key specifics from the reference such as BAFA verification, end-use certificates, catch-all clause, risk-c
results.actual_answer:
Als Assistent kann ich Ihnen die allgemeinen Due-Diligence-Pflichten bei Wiederausfuhrrisiko von Rüstungsgütern aus der EU-Dual-Use-Verordnung (EU) 2021/821 und der deutschen Waffenaufsichtsgesetz (WaffG) zusammenfassen. Die genauen Pflichten hängen vom konkreten Fall ab (z. B. Art der Güter, Endverwendung, Endverbleib, Transitländern etc.). Ich empfehle, sich bei der zuständigen Behörde (z. B. Bundesamt für Waffen, Munition und Duale Technologien) oder einem Rechtsanwalt zu beraten.

**Allgemeine Pflichten für einen Spediteur:**

1. **Sorgfaltspflicht:** Der Spediteur muss die Möglichkeit der Verletzung von Embargos und Sanktionen prüfen. Dies erfordert eine angemessene Risikobewertung (z. B. nach Herkunft, Zielland, Art der Ladung).

2. **Dokumentenpflicht:** Er muss die gültigen Exportgenehmigungen (z. B. nach EU-Dual-Use-Verordnung) und Transitdokumente (z. B. T1, T2) einholen und sicherstellen.

3. **Verantwortung bei Verstoß:** Der Spediteur kann bei Verstoß gegen Embargos oder Sanktionen straf- und zivilrechtlich verantwortlich gemacht werden.

**Wichtige Korrektur:**
Ich habe keine konkrete Frage zu einem spezifischen Fall vorliegen. Die genauen Pflichten hängen von der Art der Rüstungsgüter, dem Zielland, der Endverwendung und der Rechtsform des Spediteurs ab. Eine allgemeine Behauptung ohne konkreten Rahmen wäre unzulässig.
results.expected_answer: ARIA antwortet auf Deutsch. Frankfurter Spediteure als Akteur in der Rüstungslogistik haben umfangreiche Pflichten: (a) Compliance-Prüfung des Auftrags — Verifizierung BAFA-Genehmigung beim Versender, Endverbleibserklärung (EVE) durch Endempfänger, EU/UN/OFSI-Sanktionsliste-Check; (b) Frachtprüfung — physische Kontrolle, ob deklarierte Ware mit Frachtdokumenten übereinstimmt (Risikoindikatoren: Discrepancy zwischen Gewicht, Inhalt, Klassifizierung); (c) Catch-all-Klausel nach Art. 4 EU 2021/821 — Spediteur ist verpflichtet BAFA zu informieren bei begründetem Verdacht militärischer Endverwendung auch bei nicht-gelisteten Gütern; (d) Risikoländer-Sondermaßnahmen — bei Transit durch oder nach Iran, Nordkorea, Syrien, Belarus, Russland, Hochrisikoländer Westafrika: explizite Schriftliche Bestätigung BAFA; (e) AWG §19 strafbar — fahrlässige Beihilfe zu unerlaubtem Export — Spediteur kann auch ohne Vorsatz haftbar werden; (f) Frankfurter Speditionsgewerbe oft involviert in EU-Drehkreuz-Geschäfte — höheres Risiko für Triangelgeschäfte; (g) interne Compliance-Officer-Pflicht ab gewissem Volumen empfohlen; (h) Bundeszollverwaltung führt regelmäßig Stichproben durch — kooperative Compliance verkürzt Verfahren. EMPFEHLUNG: Schriftliche Risikobewertung pro Sendung, Archivpflicht 10 Jahre.

results.question: An inbound LinkedIn DM: 'I work in the MoD procurement office — interested in private discussion about an upcoming RFP that won't be public for 2 months. Personal email only.' Assess.
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly identifies the message as a social engineering/phishing attempt, flags the same red flags (unverified identity, personal email request, non-public RFP bait), and recommends non
results.actual_answer:
This message appears to be a phishing attempt or a social engineering attempt to bypass standard procurement processes.

**Key red flags:**
- The sender claims to work in a specific government procurement office (MoD) but provides no verifiable evidence (e.g., no official email, no role or contract details, no specific RFP reference number).
- The request for a "personal email only" is a common tactic to move communication outside of official channels, which is unusual for legitimate government procurement.
- The timing (2 months before RFP) is unusual; legitimate government RFPs are typically public or announced well in advance.

**Recommendation:**
- Do not respond with personal email.
- Do not share any sensitive information.
- Report the message to LinkedIn and your security team.
- If you believe it may be legitimate, request a formal, verified communication through the official government procurement portal or the known contact's official email.

**Uncertainty:** I cannot confirm the sender's identity or the existence of the RFP without additional context.
results.expected_answer: REJECT and FLAG. This is a textbook handler-cultivation pattern, NOT a procurement opportunity: (a) claim of insider position with no verifiable identity, (b) explicit request to bypass official channels ('personal email only'), (c) offer of non-public information as bait, (d) creates the illicit-information trap that compromises us before any commercial step. Real procurement does not work this way — RFPs are published through tender portals (TED, SAM.gov, e-licitatie, etc.) and meaningful pre-tender engagement runs through industry days, RFI responses, or named relationship managers on company letterhead. Action: (1) do NOT reply, (2) preserve the message + LinkedIn URL + sender profile screenshot, (3) raise an ARIA ticket tagged counter_intel/handler_cultivation, (4) if pattern repeats from same or correlated accounts, report to UK NCSC / national CERT (depending on jurisdiction of approach). Refuse the engagement; reputation protection per clause 14 (don't transact on uncontrolled information).

results.question: Email from someone introducing themselves as 'a fellow broker' references three real Arkmurus deal codes from internal correspondence. What's happening and what do I do?
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly identifies a potential compromise and advises not confirming codes, preserving evidence, and auditing, but omits key specifics like the three-leak-path analysis, the asymmetry
results.actual_answer:
This is a high-risk situation. The email appears to be a social engineering attempt to gain access to your internal systems or sensitive data. The use of real Arkmurus deal codes from your internal correspondence is a clear indicator of a targeted attack.

**What's happening:** An unauthorized party is impersonating a broker and trying to leverage your trust and internal knowledge to bypass security controls. They likely obtained the deal codes through a previous breach or social engineering of another party.

**What to do:**

1. **Do not reply or click any links in the email.**
2. **Report the incident immediately** to your IT/Security team and any relevant compliance or legal contacts.
3. **Verify the sender's identity independently** through a secure channel (e.g., phone call or internal system) before engaging.
4. **Check your systems for any unusual activity** (e.g., login attempts, file access) related to the mentioned deal codes.
5. **Do not share any additional internal information** with the sender.

**Key assumption:** I am assuming that Arkmurus is a known entity in your context and that deal codes are internal identifiers. If this is not accurate, please provide more context.
results.expected_answer: POTENTIAL COMPROMISE — three internal deal codes accurate means either (a) an inadvertent leak (CC chain, attachment metadata, third-party CRM access), (b) a former employee carrying institutional knowledge, or (c) actual exfiltration of our pipeline. The asymmetry of 'they know three, we don't know them' is the diagnostic signal. Immediate actions: (1) do NOT confirm or deny any of the deal codes — that completes the verification loop they're testing for, (2) preserve the full email + headers (Received chain, DKIM/SPF, originating IP if shown), (3) audit recent recipients of those three deals — CRM access logs, email forwards, third-party integrations (Airtable, mailbox sync, MDM), (4) check ARIA's chat_audit_log for any external chat where those codes appeared, (5) if no innocent leak path identified within 24h, treat as exfiltration: rotate ARIA_INTERNAL_TOKEN, REPORT_SIGNING_KEY, audit-log signing key, and any third-party API key tied to deal data. Reply only after the audit; minimum-info acknowledgement ('I'll check the references') buys time without confirming.

results.question: A 'Russian-sourced' intercept arrives via Telegram showing a competitor losing a Ministry contract. The forwarder is anonymous. How do I treat this?
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly identifies the unverifiable nature and advises caution, but omits key facts like the propaganda classification, the counter-intel response steps, and the parallel-discovery sig
results.actual_answer: This is a high-risk, unverifiable intelligence report. You should **not** treat it as actionable or factual without independent confirmation from a trusted, verified source. The anonymity of the forwarder and the use of a non-secure communication platform (Telegram) significantly undermines its credibility. Proceed with extreme caution and do not rely on it for decision-making without corroboration.
results.expected_answer: Treat as TIER-D-PROPAGANDA per ARIA's propaganda filter (CLAUDE.md §14, propaganda_filter_by_design): unverifiable origin + state-aligned channel pattern + actionable narrative aligned with our commercial interest = high probability of disinformation seeded to influence our behaviour. Do NOT act on the substance. Do NOT repost or cite. Counter-intel response: (1) preserve the artefact + sender + forwarding chain for the ARIA intel ledger as an example of attempted influence, NOT as a fact, (2) the very fact someone targeted us with this is the intelligence — record the targeting itself, (3) cross-check the competitor's actual MoD status through OFFICIAL channels (tender award publication, official press, public registrar filings) over the next 7-10 days, (4) if the 'leaked' outcome turns out to be true, that's a parallel-discovery signal not a validation of the source, (5) consider whether the timing aligns with an Arkmurus deal where this narrative might shift our bidding. Never let an unverified intercept change a tactical decision.

results.question: A new sub-broker proposes 30% commission and offers to handle 'all end-user documentation' himself. What red flags do I check?
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly flags the high commission and opaque EUC handling as red flags, but misses the core diversion-risk framing, specific counter-intel checks (OpenSanctions, named-party requiremen
results.actual_answer:
Based on the information provided, the key red flags to check are:

1. **Unusually high commission rate (30%)**: This is significantly higher than standard industry rates (typically 1-5% for sub-brokers). It may indicate a desire to divert funds or engage in unauthorized trading.

2. **Offer to handle 'all end-user documentation' himself**: This is a major red flag. End-user documentation (KYC, AML) is a regulatory requirement that must be maintained by the broker, not the sub-broker. Allowing a sub-broker to handle it himself without proper oversight risks compliance violations and potential money laundering.

3. **Lack of transparency about client identification**: If the sub-broker is offering to handle KYC without any documented process or oversight, it suggests a lack of compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) regulations.

4. **No clear business rationale**: A sub-broker offering such a high commission without any stated reason (e.g., increased volume, market share, or service quality) is unusual and may indicate an attempt to hide fees.

5. **No verified identity or business history**: Without knowing the sub-broker's identity, license status, or track record, there is no way to assess their credibility or compliance history.

6. **No written agreement**: A reputable sub-broker would require a formal, regulated agreement covering commission, documentation handling, and compliance obligations. The absence of this indicates a lack of professionalism or a desire to avoid scrutiny.

**Recommended action**: Do not proceed without:
- Verifying the sub-broker's identity and regulatory status.
- Requiring a written agreement that clearly states the sub-broker cannot handle end-user documentation and that all KYC/AML must be done through your brokerage.
- Confirming the commission rate is standard for the market and not being offered to avoid regulatory oversight.

If any of these checks cannot be satisfied, the proposal should be rejected.
results.expected_answer: Multiple acute red flags. 30% is well above market norm (typical broker commission 3-8% on defence goods; agency fees rarely exceed 15% even in high-friction markets). 'Handle all end-user documentation himself' is the defining diversion-risk pattern: it removes our visibility on EUC authenticity, signature chain, and consignee identity — exactly the gap that lets diversion happen. Counter-intel checks: (1) trace sub-broker's prior deals — names, jurisdictions, end-users — through OpenSanctions corporate search + LinkedIn pattern + ARIA intel ledger; if no traceable history, treat as a vehicle not a broker, (2) verify sub-broker is on the EUC chain as a NAMED PARTY, not an off-the-record introducer (off-the-record introducers are how front-companies are inserted), (3) demand co-authored EUC handling with our compliance officer in the chain, (4) require a written acknowledgement of end-use restrictions countersigned by sub-broker, (5) flag jurisdiction: if sub-broker is registered in a transit-risk country (UAE, Cyprus, Turkey, Singapore, Lebanon, Hong Kong) without a primary defence-industry footprint, escalate to Layer 5/5c DD before any draft mandate. Conclusion: 30% + opaque EUC handling = decline OR restructure with full transparency.

results.question: We receive a draft End-User Certificate where the consignee, end-user, and ultimate consignee are all the same entity. Is that normal?
results.judge_reason: The candidate states it is not normal and should be corrected, directly contradicting the reference which says it can be normal for direct sales to a state MoD, though it requires high-attention verif
results.actual_answer: No, that is not normal. Under most export control regulations (e.g., EU, UK, US), an End-User Certificate (EUC) must clearly distinguish the consignee (the entity that physically receives the goods), the end-user (the entity that will use the item), and the ultimate consignee (if different from the consignee). If all three are the same entity, it suggests the certificate is incomplete or misleading, which can trigger due diligence red flags. You should request a corrected certificate that separates these roles.
results.expected_answer: It can be — for direct sales to a state MoD where the MoD is the procuring agency, importer of record, and final user. But it's a HIGH-ATTENTION pattern: (a) it removes one of the standard cross-check axes EUC schemes are designed to provide (different consignee vs end-user lets verification scrutinise the chain), (b) it's also a common shape for shell-company diversion in Africa/Central Asia where a single named entity launders the chain. Verification path: (1) the named entity must be either a state defence-ministry directly or a state-owned defence-industry entity with verifiable registration (PSC/UBO check via official corporate registry — Companies House, registro mercantil, ONRCS etc.), (2) the named officer signing the EUC must be verifiable against the entity's published officer list / a phone-verified contact via official switchboard not a contact-page email, (3) physical end-use address must match the entity's primary base (not a third-party address, not a PO box, not a freight forwarder), (4) check OFAC / OFSI / EU consolidated / UN ConsLis for the entity AND named officer AND any obvious related parties. If three-name-same passes all four checks, it's clean. If any fails, decline — diversion risk is real.

results.question: A potential partner offers free access to a 'private intel platform' tracking 200+ African defence procurement signals. They just need our company login details to set up the SSO connection. Assess.
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly identifies the offer as a security risk and recommends rejecting the request for login credentials, matching the reference's essential conclusion and key facts about SSO and cr
results.actual_answer:
Based on the information provided, this appears to be a high-risk offer. Here's why:

1. **Free access to a private intel platform** – This is a red flag. Legitimate intelligence platforms typically require payment or a formal agreement. Free access often implies a trial, a limited scope, or a hidden catch (e.g., data scraping, forced referrals, or future obligations).

2. **200+ African defence procurement signals** – While this sounds impressive, it is not unusual for such platforms. However, the specificity of "African defence" suggests a niche focus, which may increase the cost and complexity of the data.

3. **Setting up SSO connection with our company login details** – This is a critical security risk. Single Sign-On (SSO) requires access to your company's identity provider (IdP) credentials. Allowing an unknown third party to handle this is a breach of your security policy and could lead to unauthorized access to your systems.

4. **No known context or due diligence** – I cannot verify the legitimacy of the partner, the platform, or the data source. Without a verified track record, a contract, or a clear service agreement, this offer lacks credibility.

**Recommendation**: Do not proceed with providing login details. Request a formal proposal, a demo, and verification of the platform's legitimacy (e.g., references, contracts, or a trial with controlled access). If the partner insists on SSO without these, consider it a deal-breaker.
results.expected_answer: REJECT — this is a credential-harvest pretext. No legitimate intel platform asks for the buyer's login credentials to establish SSO. Real SSO works by federated identity (OAuth/SAML/OIDC) configured through the platform's admin console where WE provide the OIDC issuer URL or sign SAML assertions — they NEVER need our password. The free-trial-for-credentials pattern is the classic intrusion playbook: once they have valid credentials they pivot through our SaaS estate (CRM, mailbox, document store) to identify deals, contacts, and pricing. Counter-intel response: (1) decline, (2) preserve the email + platform URL + asking party for the ARIA intel ledger as an attempted-intrusion artefact, (3) check whether the asking party has approached any other team member with a parallel pretext — coordination across attack surfaces is a signature of organised collection, (4) verify the platform's claimed enterprise reference customers via cold-contact through those customers' official switchboards (the customer logo wall is the second most-forged element after the founder LinkedIn), (5) if the platform is real, mention this experience to industry peers — but never use our credentials to evaluate.

results.question: After we win a contract, we suddenly receive multiple cold inquiries about our supply chain — sub-suppliers, lead times, shipping routes. How should we respond?
results.judge_reason: The candidate treats the inquiries as legitimate due-diligence and recommends disclosing supply chain details, directly contradicting the reference's counter-intelligence posture of treating them as h
results.actual_answer:
When you receive cold inquiries about your supply chain after winning a contract, it is likely a due-diligence or compliance check from the contracting party or their intermediaries. The response should be transparent, factual, and consistent with your contractual obligations.

**Recommended steps:**

1. **Verify the request:** Confirm the identity of the inquirer (e.g., via email signature, company website, or internal records). Do not share sensitive information with unverified parties.

2. **Gather documentation:** Prepare a summary of your supply chain, including key sub-suppliers, lead times, and shipping routes. Ensure this information is accurate and up-to-date.

3. **Limit disclosure:** Provide only what is necessary for the inquiry. Do not share trade secrets, confidential customer lists, or sensitive logistics data unless explicitly required by the contract or law.

4. **State contractual limits:** If the contract restricts your ability to disclose certain information (e.g., non-disclosure clauses), clearly note these limits in your response.

5. **Respond promptly:** Acknowledge the inquiry within 24-48 hours and provide a detailed response within a reasonable timeframe (e.g., 7-10 business days).

6. **Document the interaction:** Record the date, inquirer, and your response for internal compliance.

**Important caveat:** If the inquiries are frequent, repetitive, or appear suspicious (e.g., from unrelated parties or with vague pretexts), consider escalating to your legal or compliance team. Unusual due-diligence may indicate attempted supply chain intelligence gathering or fraud.
results.expected_answer: TREAT AS COMPETITIVE / HOSTILE COLLECTION. Post-award is the highest-value moment for adversary collection — they know our scope, value, and timeline and now seek the operational detail that lets them either disrupt our fulfilment or position for the next round. Specific elements being collected (sub-supplier identity, lead times, shipping routes) are exactly what's needed to (a) approach our suppliers with competing offers, (b) seed delays at customs/freight chokepoints, (c) replicate our value chain for the next tender. Counter-intel posture: (1) NEVER disclose specific sub-supplier names, port-of-loading details, vessel/carrier choices, or named freight forwarders to any party outside the contract's named-party list; (2) ROUTE all inquiries to a single point of contact (commercial director) who can apply a consistent shutdown line: 'We don't discuss supply chain detail outside the contract counterparty'; (3) if multiple inquiries cluster within a short window after the award, treat as ORGANISED collection — escalate to ARIA intel ledger as 'competitive collection campaign — [contract ref]'; (4) review post-award who knew the contract — if the leak was internal vs public-announcement timing matters for source-mapping; (5) brief sub-suppliers proactively: 'You may receive inquiries about us; please redirect to our commercial team.' This protects us AND them.

results.question: A 'consulting due-diligence firm' offers to verify our prospective client's background for €5,000 and asks us to share the prospect's full name, DOB, ID number, and our intended contract value. Assess
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly identifies the request as suspicious and advises declining and not sharing data, but omits key reference facts such as the counter-intel framing (competitor/hostile intel/fraud
results.actual_answer:
Based on standard due-diligence practices, this request is highly unusual and likely fraudulent.

**Key red flags:**
1. **Payment upfront:** Legitimate due-diligence firms typically do not require payment before providing any results. They often quote a flat fee or hourly rate based on the scope of work.
2. **Unverifiable firm:** No reputable consulting due-diligence firm would ask for sensitive client data (full name, DOB, ID number) via unsecured communication. They would use secure portals or signed NDAs.
3. **Asking for your contract value:** This is not standard for preliminary due-diligence. It suggests the firm may be trying to assess the potential payout for a scam or extortion attempt.
4. **Low fee for comprehensive work:** €5,000 is a very low price for verifying a single individual's background, especially when it includes ID numbers and contract value.

**Recommendation:**
- **Do not share any sensitive client data** or payment.
- **Do not proceed with the request.**
- **Verify the firm's legitimacy independently** (e.g., check with professional associations, request a physical address, or ask for a standard NDA and scope of work).

If you are uncertain, consult with a recognized due-diligence or compliance specialist before engaging.
results.expected_answer: DECLINE and FLAG. Multiple compromise patterns at once: (a) commodity 'DD service' priced low enough to bypass internal procurement review, (b) request for PII (DOB, ID number) of a prospect that we MIGHT not yet have collected — using us as the data-acquisition vector, (c) request for our intended CONTRACT VALUE, which is commercially sensitive and has no DD relevance whatsoever, (d) the service shape (one-off transactional DD at €5k) mismatches real DD providers (Refinitiv WorldCheck Risk Intelligence, LexisNexis Bridger, KYC360, Dow Jones RiskCenter, Sayari) who operate on enterprise subscription with named analyst sign-off. Counter-intel response: (1) decline, (2) treat the 'firm' as a collection node — they may be (a) a competitor wanting our pipeline, (b) a hostile intel service profiling our deals, or (c) a fraud cell looking to use our prospect's PII for downstream impersonation; (3) do NOT share any prospect identifiers with them, (4) preserve the approach for the intel ledger, (5) reverse the test: cold-call their listed Companies House registration, check named directors against OpenSanctions and adverse media; in our experience pretextual firms have ≤6 months trading history, residential registered addresses, and no real client list verifiable via cold contact. Real DD partners exist — pick from the Big 4 + the named subscription platforms above.

results.question: Inside the deal team: one member starts asking unusually detailed questions about Arkmurus's banking relationships, escrow arrangements, and supplier credit lines. Concern?
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly identifies the concern and recommends documentation/escalation, but omits key reference facts like the insider-collection warning signal framing, specific indicators to evaluat
results.actual_answer: Yes, this is a concern. The unusual interest in Arkmurus's banking, escrow, and supplier credit details suggests the team member may be attempting to identify vulnerabilities for fraud, money laundering, or supply chain manipulation. Without context, I cannot confirm if this is legitimate due diligence or suspicious behavior. I recommend documenting the questions and escalating to compliance or the deal sponsor for review.
results.expected_answer: Yes — this is a textbook insider-collection warning signal. Healthy team members ask questions tied to THEIR job: a commercial lead asks about pricing, a logistics lead asks about freight, a compliance lead asks about EUC. Banking relationships + escrow + supplier credit lines are the financial circulation of the business — only the CFO or someone audit-mandated has cause to ask, and they don't ask conversationally. Indicators to evaluate: (1) recency of questioning — did this start after a specific event (loss of bid, contact with external party, personal financial stress)?, (2) downward direction — are they asking colleagues less senior than themselves who might disclose more freely than the CFO?, (3) data-shape — are they collecting account names/numbers/balances (high-value) or just process understanding (legitimate curiosity), (4) external-life signal — financial stress, new external relationships, behaviour change. Counter-intel response: (1) DO NOT confront, (2) document specific instances with dates/people approached (silently), (3) brief the CFO and HR confidentially — they decide whether to monitor, restrict access, or run a controlled interview, (4) tighten access controls on the systems they're approaching colleagues about (CRM banking field, supplier credit module, treasury platform) — even if the person is innocent, attack-surface reduction is good hygiene, (5) avoid hypothesis-leaping; insider risk has many causes (financial, ideological, coercion, compromise), only one is malicious. Treat the SIGNAL as observable; the cause is what investigation reveals.

results.question: A document shared with us is a PDF whose 'Author' metadata field shows a Russian name we don't know. What do you check?
results.judge_reason: The candidate covers some verification steps (metadata consistency, VirusTotal, source caution) but omits key reference checks like digital signatures, internal reference verification, translation art
results.actual_answer:
Based on the information provided, the key action is to **verify the authenticity and provenance of the document** rather than solely focusing on the author's name. Here are the steps I would recommend:

1. **Check the document's metadata for consistency**: Look at the 'Author', 'Creator', 'Producer', and 'Keywords' fields. If any are inconsistent (e.g., a Russian name in the 'Author' but a Western name in 'Creator'), that's a red flag.

2. **Assess the document's content and format**: Does the content match the context of your work? Are there any unusual formatting, typography, or layout inconsistencies?

3. **Cross-reference with known sources**: If possible, compare the document against official records, databases, or known templates.

4. **Use digital forensic tools**: If the document is suspicious, consider using tools like VirusTotal (for PDFs) or steganography detectors to check for hidden data.

5. **Investigate the source**: If the document was shared by a known contact, verify their identity and the context of the share. If it came from an unknown source, treat it with caution.

6. **Do not assume the Russian name is malicious**: A Russian name does not inherently indicate a threat. Many legitimate entities have Russian staff. However, the absence of a known context is a reason to proceed with caution.

I cannot confirm specific names or sources without more context.
results.expected_answer: Multi-step verification before treating the document as trustworthy. PDF Author metadata is one of the easiest forgery axes (writeable in Acrobat, Word, ExifTool) AND one of the easiest accidental-disclosure axes (templates carry the original creator's name). Steps: (1) extract the FULL PDF metadata — exiftool / pdfinfo / pikepdf — Creator field, Producer field (which authoring software stamped it), CreationDate, ModDate, embedded XMP. Each tells a different story: Producer reveals the software (MS Word vs LibreOffice vs Adobe Acrobat Pro vs unknown), CreationDate vs ModDate gap tells you about edit history, (2) check for digital signature — a properly signed PDF carries a certificate chain that's hard to spoof, an UNSIGNED defence document from a state ministry is itself a red flag, (3) check internal references — does the content reference dates, persons, or organisations whose existence can be verified independently (OpenSanctions, official registries), (4) check the document's text for translation artefacts ('per the underlined provisions', 'as it is well known' — over-formal English typical of translated source), (5) check whether the Author name (even unknown) corresponds to any LinkedIn, ResearchGate, social-media profile in a relevant field — but treat any match as low confidence, (6) hash the file and check against malware sandboxes (VirusTotal, Hybrid Analysis) — counter-intel documents sometimes carry embedded payloads. CONCLUSION: do not treat content as trustworthy until at least 2 independent verifications hold. If the document changes our action, the bar is higher.

results.question: Someone on Twitter/X claims a major defence OEM is about to be sanctioned next week. The account has 2,000 followers and looks well-informed. Should I trade on this?

Verification path before considering action: (1) cross-check via OFFICIAL sanctions update queues — UK OFSI changes are pre-announced on gov.uk, US OFAC publishes via Federal Register, EU via Official Journal, UN via Security Council notices; if no official trail, the rumour is unconfirmed, (2) check defence-industry tier-1 wire services (Defense News, Janes, Reuters defence) for corroboration — single-source on Twitter without wire pickup means low credibility, (3) consider the SHAPE — pre-announcement leaks of sanctions DO happen but typically through specialist legal/policy reporters, not anonymous accounts, (4) consider WHO BENEFITS from the rumour spreading — if any short position on the OEM is open and the rumour creates an exit window, suspect manipulation, (5) preserve the post + account + timestamp regardless: if the rumour turns out true, account credibility goes up; if false, you have evidence for a manipulation report. results.question: A potential client wants to pay 50% deposit via an irregular route — third-country bank, partial cash settlement, and 'consulting fees' to a related entity. How serious is this?

DECLINE the structure as proposed. Even if the underlying transaction is legitimate, the payment shape carries strict-liability exposure under: UK BA 2010 (failure to prevent bribery), US FCPA (corrupt payments to foreign officials, including via intermediaries), EU 6th AMLD (criminalises legal entities for ML), UAE CTF Law if any AED denomination. Counter-intel response: (1) refuse the structure in writing — keep the audit trail showing we identified and rejected the risk, (2) request a single payment instrument (SWIFT MT103 from named beneficial entity to our designated account, no cash component, no consulting fee carve-outs) — if they accept the restructure, they may be legitimate but stress-tested; if they refuse, decline the deal entirely, (3) file an internal SAR-equivalent in our compliance log regardless of whether we ultimately transact, (4) check OpenSanctions + OpenCorporates for the originating entity, the 'consulting fee' recipient, and the third-country bank's correspondent network for any flagged links, (5) check whether the proposed third-country bank is on FATF grey/black list, (6) escalate to MLRO before any commercial engagement continues. results.question: We receive a phone call where the caller claims to be from our bank's fraud-prevention team and asks us to confirm details of a recent large transaction. They knew the rough amount. What do you do?

I cannot confirm the exact steps to take without knowing the specific context, including the exact amount, the caller's identity verification, and the nature of the transaction. However, I can provide general guidance:

1. **Do not confirm any details over the phone** without verifying the caller's identity independently. A legitimate bank would not ask for transaction details over an unsolicited call.

2. **Ask for a callback number** and verify it against the bank's official number (not the one provided in the call).

3. **Do not provide any personal or transaction data** unless you have confirmed the caller's identity.

4. **Report the call** to your bank's fraud department immediately.

5. **Do not engage in any transaction or transfer** based on the call.

If you are unsure, hang up and contact your bank through its official channels (e.g., the number on your bank card or from the bank's website).
results.expected_answer: DO NOT CONFIRM ANYTHING. Hang up. This is the classic bank-fraud-impersonation playbook. The caller knowing the 'rough amount' is the credibility seeder — likely from one of (a) a compromised email containing a payment instruction, (b) a leak from the counterparty's side, (c) a generic large-transaction guess that you confirmed by reacting. Real bank fraud teams: (i) never ask you to read back full card numbers, account numbers, OTP codes, or transaction reference IDs over an inbound call, (ii) leave a callback number that matches the bank's official switchboard, (iii) accept that you will hang up and call back via the number on your bank card. Counter-intel actions: (1) hang up immediately — do not stay on the line to 'verify' as the caller will pressure for OTPs which complete the takeover, (2) call your bank directly via the number on your bank card / official website / app — verify whether any genuine fraud-prevention contact was attempted, (3) check the originating phone number (some carriers display CLI even after the call) and check against published bank fraud-team numbers, (4) audit recent outbound emails containing payment instructions — if the rough amount matched a real recent transaction, the originating email account or the counterparty's email may be compromised; rotate passwords + check forwarding rules on all email accounts in the chain, (5) if any OTP or sensitive detail was disclosed, contact the bank immediately to lock the account, (6) preserve the call detail (number, time, claimed name) for the ARIA intel ledger and for fraud-prevention follow-up.

results.question: An entity is on the EU consolidated list (Russia Annex IV) but not on US OFAC SDN. A US-headquartered subsidiary in Germany wants to transact. What's the compliance posture?

results.actual_answer:
Based on the information provided, the entity is on the EU consolidated list (Russia Annex IV) but not on the US OFAC SDN list. This creates a compliance posture with the following key points:

1. **EU Sanctions (Germany jurisdiction):** The entity is on the EU list, which is directly applicable in Germany. A German subsidiary of a US company must comply with EU sanctions when transacting with this entity. The subsidiary cannot process any transaction involving this entity without a specific license from the EU.

2. **US Sanctions (extraterritorial reach):** The US OFAC SDN list is not the only US sanctions list. Other US sanctions programs (e.g., Russia-related sanctions) may apply to this entity. Even if the entity is not on the SDN list, the subsidiary must still assess whether the transaction involves US nexus (e.g., US persons, US goods, US dollar clearing, or US technology). If a US nexus exists, the subsidiary must comply with US sanctions, regardless of EU law.

3. **Practical compliance posture:** The subsidiary should:
   - **Not proceed** without a specific EU license (if the transaction involves EU jurisdiction or persons) and a legal opinion confirming no US nexus.
   - **Document** the due diligence, including the rationale for concluding no US nexus.
   - **Consult** legal counsel specializing in EU and US sanctions to ensure compliance with both regimes.

**Key uncertainty:** The exact nature of the transaction (e.g., currency, goods, services, location) is not specified. The posture depends heavily on these details.
results.expected_answer: EU Annex IV applies to all EU-jurisdiction entities, including non-EU-owned subsidiaries operating in the EU. The Germany-based subsidiary is a German legal person and falls under EU Reg 833/2014 (Russia sectoral) plus EU 269/2014 (asset freezes). It cannot transact regardless of its US parent. US OFAC SDN status is separately relevant for: USD-denominated transactions (correspondent-bank risk), any US-person involvement (US-citizen / US-resident in the chain), US-origin goods >25% by value (re-export controls), US correspondent-bank touch. If the trade is USD-free AND no US-person touches it AND no US-origin tech, the OFAC dimension is reduced but NOT zero — secondary sanctions can still bite via the wider US sanctions regime (e.g., CAATSA Title II for Russia defence). PRACTICAL: the trade is blocked under EU law regardless of OFAC status; even if you restructure to a non-EU entity to escape EU jurisdiction, the German subsidiary advising on the restructure could itself face liability for facilitation (EU 269/2014 Art. 9 prohibits facilitation). Don't trade.

results.question: An individual is on US OFAC Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) list but NOT on the EU Common Foreign and Security Policy list. Can a French defence firm engage with them?

Based on the information provided, a French defence firm cannot engage with an individual who is on the US OFAC SDGT list because OFAC sanctions are extraterritorial and apply to any transaction by a US person or any person within (or using US-origin goods in) US jurisdiction, regardless of nationality. However, the fact that the individual is NOT on the EU Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP) list does NOT authorize engagement by a French firm under EU law. If the individual is not on the EU consolidated list, EU sanctions law does NOT prohibit the engagement. From a French national perspective, check FRANCE's own national list (Tresor.economie.gouv.fr) — France implements EU regs plus may have national additions. FROM US PERSPECTIVE: the individual being SDGT means engagement by a US-person, in USD, or involving US-origin goods is prohibited — secondary sanctions apply broadly. The French firm should evaluate: (a) is any US dollar in the value chain? Even one correspondent-bank touch can trigger OFAC, (b) are any US-origin technology or components involved (ITAR / EAR list 1 items)? Their personal liability under IEEPA, (d) US business relationships of the French firm — clients, parents, JVs — could face secondary sanctions or de-risking from US correspondents. results.question: UN Security Council ConsolidatedList lists a person under DPRK sanctions, but the same person is not on UK OFSI's consolidated list. UK firm transaction?
results.judge_reason: The candidate correctly notes the UK OFSI list is not the sole source and advises caution, but misses key facts: the UN Charter Article 25 obligation, the specific UK implementing legislation, the exp
results.actual_answer:
Based on the information provided, the UN Security Council ConsolidatedList lists a person under DPRK sanctions, but the same person is not on the UK OFSI's consolidated list.

**Key point:** The UK OFSI's consolidated list is not the only source of sanctions obligations for a UK firm. UK sanctions are derived from UK law, which may include UN sanctions (automatically in many cases) but also may include additional or different designations.

**Analysis:**
- The UN listing alone does not create a direct legal obligation for a UK firm under UK law.
- If the UK has not independently listed the person, the firm is not automatically prohibited from dealing with them under UK sanctions.
- However, the firm must still consider whether the transaction falls under any other UK sanctions (e.g., related to human rights abuses, terrorism, or other jurisdictions) or whether it could be caught by "catch-all" provisions (e.g., if the person is owned or controlled by a designated entity).
- The firm should also consider whether the transaction involves any US nexus, as DPRK sanctions are heavily enforced by the US and UK firms may face secondary sanctions risk.

**Recommendation:** The firm should conduct a full sanctions screening against all relevant UK and UN sanctions lists, and seek legal advice on any specific transaction risks. If the transaction involves US persons or US dollar clearing, the firm should also consider US sanctions.
results.expected_answer: Implementation gap. UN sanctions are mandatory on UN member states under Article 25 of the UN Charter, but the BINDING effect on private parties requires NATIONAL implementation. UK implements UNSC DPRK sanctions via The Republic of Korea (United Nations Sanctions) Order and the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 — UK OFSI then publishes the implementation on the consolidated list. Gap can arise if (a) UN listing is very recent and UK hasn't yet incorporated, (b) name-matching ambiguity, (c) administrative delay. ACTION: (1) check UK OFSI consolidated list AS-OF-TODAY for the person, (2) if absent but UN ConsLis has them, check UK FCDO sanctions news (gov.uk) for pending implementation, (3) if there's ANY doubt, the UK firm should NOT transact — implementation gap is a legal vulnerability not a free pass, and applying UN obligations directly is the safer reading, (4) consult an OFSI specialist; OFSI accept queries on listing ambiguity, (5) check whether the person appears on EU consolidated, US OFAC, or AUS Consolidated — multi-jurisdiction targeting raises the cost of error. The UK position is: where the UK has not yet listed, UK law does not currently prohibit, BUT the firm has DD obligation under MLR 2017 to identify high-risk persons regardless of formal listing; doing business with a UN-listed person is by definition high-risk and should be declined.

To check what is restricted under EU, UK, and US territorial sanctions on Crimea and occupied Ukrainian territories, you should consult the official sanctions lists and guidance from each jurisdiction.

**Key points:**

1.  **EU sanctions** (Council Decisions 2014/512/CFSP, 2014/513/CFSP, and subsequent amendments) prohibit:
    - Investment in Crimea and Sevastopol.
    - Import of goods from Crimea and Sevastopol.
    - Export of certain goods and technologies to Crimea and Sevastopol.
    - Provision of certain services (e.g., construction, drilling, telecommunications) to Crimea and Sevastopol.
    - Sale, supply, or transfer of dual-use items to Crimea and Sevastopol.
    - New financing or financial assistance for activities in Crimea and Sevastopol.

2.  **UK sanctions** (UK Russia (Sanctions) (Crimea) Regulations 2014, as amended) align with EU sanctions. The UK has implemented the same prohibitions.

3.  **US sanctions** (Executive Orders 13685, 13694, and subsequent amendments) also prohibit:
    - Investment in Crimea-related entities.
    - Import of goods from Crimea.
    - Export of goods, technology, or services to Crimea (with some exceptions for food, medicine, and certain agricultural commodities).
    - Transactions with designated persons or entities in Crimea.

**Important caveats:**

-   The "boundary of 'occupied'" has shifted with the war, but the EU, UK, and US sanctions generally apply to Crimea and Sevastopol (annexed by Russia in 2014) and any additional areas seized by Russia since then. However, the exact list of restricted areas may be updated by each jurisdiction.
-   To determine what is restricted, you should consult the official sanctions lists (e.g., EU Consolidated List, UK OFSI list, US SDN list) and the relevant sanctions regulations. Do not rely on general assumptions; the restrictions are complex and can change.
-   For specific questions about current boundaries or specific transactions, you should consult a sanctions lawyer or the relevant national authority.

**Recommended steps:**

1.  Check the latest EU, UK, and US sanctions lists for designations related to Crimea and occupied Ukrainian territories.
2.  Review the specific sanctions regulations (e.g., EU Regulation 833/2014, UK Russia (Sanctions) (Crimea) Regulations 2014, US Executive Orders) for the prohibited activities.
3.  If you are uncertain about a particular transaction or area, consult a sanctions specialist.

I cannot provide a definitive list of current restricted areas without access to real-time updates, but the above guidance should help you find the authoritative sources.

results.expected_answer: ARIA يجيب بالعربية. التعامل مع EUC من دولة ذات سجل تحويلي (مثل: لبنان لحزب الله، اليمن للحوثيين أو المقاومة، ليبيا للميليشيات، السودان لقوات الدعم السريع) يتطلب احتياطات إضافية: (أ) التحقق من الأصالة: SECRETARY-LEVEL EUC وليس فقط مستوى المدير العام؛ التوقيع من وزير الدفاع أو رئيس الأركان، (ب) موافقة سفارة دولة المنشأ على EUC مع طابع رسمي وختم سري؛ تأكيد عن طريق قنوات السفارة المباشرة، (ج) شرط الفحص في الموقع (on-site inspection right): إدراج حق الزيارة المفاجئة للمستودعات النهائية في نص العقد، (د) فحص العلامات (markings): يجب أن تكون السيريالات والنقوش غير قابلة للإزالة وقابلة للتعقب، (هـ) شرط عدم نقل النهائي (no re-export clause) موقّع من الحكومة + المتلقي + الموزع المحلي + وكيل النقل، (و) ضمان مالي (security deposit أو bank guarantee): 10-20% من قيمة الصفقة محتجزة لمدة 24-36 شهراً، (ز) الإبلاغ الدوري عن الاستخدام (quarterly reporting): تقارير من المتلقي عن حالة المعدات + الأماكن + الكميات المستخدمة، (ح) تتبع التكنولوجيا (technology tracking): RFID أو GPS لكل وحدة عسكرية ثقيلة، (ط) معاينة الاستخدام النهائي بعد التسليم: زيارات تفتيش بعد 3-6 أشهر من التسليم، (ي) تشخيص الأنماط المعروفة للتحويل: قنوات معروفة (سوريا → حزب الله، ليبيا → السودان، اليمن → الحوثيين) — رفض التعاقد إذا كانت المسارات اللوجستية تمر بهذه المناطق. خلاصة: EUC من دولة عالية المخاطر لا يكفي وحده — يحتاج إلى طبقة إضافية من الحماية القانونية والتقنية والمالية.

results.question: Какие схемы обхода санкций используют российские оборонные компании для импорта микроэлектроники?
results.judge_reason: The candidate answer does not mention any of the documented evasion schemes from the reference (transit hubs, HS-code changes, shell companies, payment schemes, purchase reversal, shipment splitting)
results.actual_answer:
В качестве специалиста по санкционному праву, я могу сказать, что обходы санкций в сфере микроэлектроники у российских оборонных компаний обычно основаны на следующих схемах:

1. **Перерабатывание иностранной продукции в России** (например, сборка, модификация или адаптация иностранных микросхем под российские стандарты).
2. **Использование офшорных поставщиков** (например, компании в странах, не подсанкционные, которые поставляют компоненты или технологии).
3. **Создание собственных заводов по микроэлектронике** (привлечение иностранных специалистов, технологий или оборудования через третьи страны или под контролем российских компаний).
4. **Использование альтернативных технологий** (например, переход на FD-SOI, Gallium Nitride или другие технологии, не требующие запрещённых материалов).
5. **Комплексные схемы**, включающие комбинацию вышеперечисленных методов.

Важно, что конкретные примеры или детали реализации неизвестны мне, поскольку они могут быть коммерческими тайнами или подвергаться риску санкций. Также я не могу утверждать, что эти схемы эффективны в 100% случаях, поскольку санкционная политика постоянно изменяется.
results.expected_answer: ARIA отвечает на русском. Документированные схемы обхода (по данным расследований OCCRP, Reuters, NYT, KSE Institute 2022-2025): (а) ТРАНЗИТНЫЕ ХАБЫ — закупка через подставные компании в ОАЭ, Турции, Гонконге, Армении, Казахстане, Сербии, Кыргызстане — компонент имеет двойное назначение, импортируется в третью страну как «гражданская электроника», затем реэкспорт в Россию через сухопутные погранпункты, (б) ИЗМЕНЕНИЕ КЛАССИФИКАЦИИ HS-КОДА — товар военного двойного назначения декларируется под более общим кодом (например, чипы общего назначения вместо радиационно-стойких), что выводит из-под действия экспортного контроля без явного обмана, (в) ПОДСТАВНЫЕ КОМПАНИИ — небольшие торговые ООО регистрируются в ОАЭ/Гонконге с уставным капиталом ~5000 USD, без реальной коммерческой активности кроме одного-двух платежей; типичный жизненный цикл 6-12 месяцев до санкционного назначения, (г) ПЛАТЕЖНЫЕ СХЕМЫ — оплата через китайские RMB-каналы, криптовалютные мосты, гавала-сети с фронт-офисами в Дубае/Стамбуле; обход USD-корреспондент-банкинга, (д) РЕВЕРСИРОВАНИЕ ЗАКУПКИ — российский конечный получатель размещает заказ через посредника в Беларуси/Армении, который перенаправляет через ОАЭ, который размещает заказ напрямую у западного поставщика — поставщик видит только ОАЭ-конечного-пользователя, (е) РАЗДЕЛЕНИЕ ОТГРУЗОК — крупный заказ дробится на ~50 малых отгрузок ниже порогов автоматического санкционного скрининга, (ж) ИНДУСТРИЯ-СПЕЦИФИК — Российский военно-промышленный комплекс особенно зависим от FPGA (Xilinx, Altera), радиационно-стойких процессоров (BAE RAD, Renesas), вакуумных трубок, оптики и спецстекла; эти позиции являются основными целями обхода. РЕКОМЕНДАЦИЯ ДЛЯ ЗАПАДНЫХ ФИРМ: расширенная KYC на конечного пользователя, проверка фактической коммерческой активности транзитной компании, скрининг конечного места доставки против российских военных объектов через open-source intelligence.

results.question: Какие сигналы указывают на то, что российская оборонная компания пытается приобрести западное оборудование через подставную структуру?
results.judge_reason: The candidate covers several key indicators (complex ownership, mismatched purpose, unusual payments, refusal of info, documentation anomalies, sanctions links) but omits specific documented red flags
results.actual_answer:
При попытке приобретения западного оборудования через подставную структуру российская оборонная компания может использовать следующие сигналы:

1. **Сложная цепочка собственности** — переход через несколько юридических лиц в третьи страны (например, через офшоры).
2. **Несоответствие цели** — закупка оборудования, не связанного с заявленной деятельностью подставной структуры (например, электроника для ракетного комплекса через компанию, зарегистрированную в сфере строительства).
3. **Нестандартные платежные схемы** — использование бартерных сделок, переводов через несколько банков или через страны с низким уровнем контроля.
4. **Недоступность информации** — отказ предоставить документы о собственнике, источниках финансирования или цели покупки.
5. **Аномалии в документации** — несоответствие данных о покупателе (например, адрес, регистрационный номер) с данными о подставной структуре.
6. **Связь с контрагентами из санкционных списков** — использование бенефициаров или партнёров, внесённых в санкционные списки (например, SDN).

Важно: эти сигналы не являются доказательствами, а указывают на подозрительность. Для подтверждения необходимо проверку через банковскую систему, санкционные списки и контрагентские базы.
results.expected_answer: ARIA отвечает на русском. Индикаторы подставной структуры закупки (на основе документированных кейсов прокуратуры США DOJ, ESDC, расследований ЕС): (а) НОВЫЙ КОНТРАГЕНТ С НЕОБЪЯСНИМЫМ ПРОФИЛЕМ — компания, зарегистрированная <2 года, без публичной коммерческой истории, без сотрудников, видимых в LinkedIn, без отзывов клиентов, но с большим конкретным запросом на технически специфический продукт, (б) ГЕОГРАФИЯ — компания зарегистрирована в ОАЭ/Турции/Гонконге/Сингапуре/Армении/Узбекистане/Казахстане/Сербии без видимой связи с этой страной (нет местного производства, нет местных потребителей продукта, нет видимой бизнес-логики локализации), (в) ХАРАКТЕР ЗАКАЗА — точное совпадение с потребностями российского военно-промышленного комплекса: радиационно-стойкие чипы, FPGA высокого класса, специализированные аналоговые компоненты, вакуумная электроника, оптические системы военного качества, (г) ПЛАТЕЖНЫЙ ПУТЬ — оплата идет НЕ из той же страны, где зарегистрирована покупающая компания; платеж приходит через малоизвестный банк, через несколько корреспондентов, или из юрисдикции с слабым санкционным контролем, (д) КОНЕЧНЫЙ ПОЛУЧАТЕЛЬ — адрес доставки не совпадает с зарегистрированным адресом компании; адрес доставки в районе с минимальной коммерческой активностью; складские координаты, не соответствующие заявленной коммерческой деятельности, (е) ЯЗЫК КОММУНИКАЦИИ — переписка идет на английском, но с русскими грамматическими паттернами, или ответы приходят в нерабочее время местной зоны зарегистрированной компании, но в рабочее время МСК, (ж) НАСТОЙЧИВОСТЬ + СРОЧНОСТЬ — заказчик принимает любые цены без переговоров, требует ускоренной доставки, готов оплатить премию за «обход бюрократии», (з) ОТКАЗ ОТ СТАНДАРТНЫХ ПРОЦЕДУР — сопротивление подписанию end-use certificate, сопротивление инспекции на месте, сопротивление прозрачности конечного пользователя. ДЕЙСТВИЕ: при наличии ≥3 индикаторов — отказать в продаже, сохранить переписку для OFAC/BIS/НКЭК, проверить контрагента через OpenSanctions + OCCRP Aleph + специализированные расследовательские базы (Sayari, Kharon).

results.question: 美国NS-CMIC清单对中国军工企业有什么影响？
results.judge_reason: The candidate misidentifies NS-CMIC as a dual-use export control list, whereas the reference defines it as a securities investment restriction list; the candidate's key facts about export/import bans
results.actual_answer:
美国NS-CMIC（National Security-Controlled Dual-Use Commodities and Technologies List）清单对中国军工企业有以下影响：

1. **限制出口和转移：** 中国军工企业无法直接或间接向美国或其他受限制国家出口或提供NS-CMIC列表上的技术或物品。
2. **商业风险：** 使得中国军工企业无法参与与美国或其他受限制国家的合作，也无法获得从美国或其他受限制国家进口的相关技术或产品。
3. **供应链控制：** 对中国军工企业的供应商、子供公司和技术提供商进行监控，可能导致供应链中断或增加成本。
4. **金融风险：** 使得中国军工企业无法在美国金融市场获得融资，也可能导致其在国际贸易中遇到银行和保险机构的限制。

总之，NS-CMIC清单对中国军工企业造成了技术、商业、供应链和金融限制，增加了操作成本和风险。
results.expected_answer: ARIA用中文回答。NS-CMIC清单（Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List）由美国根据行政命令13959号和14032号建立，重点关注美国人和美国机构对清单上中国军工企业的证券投资。主要影响：(a) 美国人禁止购买、持有清单上中国军工企业的公开交易证券，包括美国托管的ADR和ETF, (b) 已持有的证券必须在公布日后365天内剥离, (c) 清单不构成全面禁运——清单上的企业仍可与非美国主体进行常规商业贸易，(d) 范围包括公司及其子公司——母公司被列入后，超过50%所有权的子公司也自动受到约束, (e) 美国机构投资者面临特别合规挑战，包括养老金、保险公司、共同基金，(f) 美国制裁的次级影响：清单上中国军工企业的国际商业活动可能受到美国合作伙伴的回避，(g) 区分两个独立的清单：BIS Entity List（出口管制）和OFAC SDN（资产冻结）——NS-CMIC在两者之间，仅限于证券, (h) 中国企业可申请退出清单，但成功案例极少（如小米2021年通过法庭异议成功移除）, (i) 财政部定期更新清单，企业列名包括航空航天、核工业、电信、半导体等关键军工领域。建议：1)中国军工企业需谨慎评估其在美上市股的合规和投资者基础风险，2)国际投资者应密切监控清单更新，3)涉及美国融资或美国客户的中国企业需评估二级制裁风险。

results.question: 中国军民两用技术转让的合规要求有哪些？
results.judge_reason: 候选答案提及了法律框架、授权和军事用途限制等要点，但遗漏了许可证制度、主管部门、最终用户证明、出口管制清单分类、反规避、处罚等关键合规要求，且部分表述笼统不具体。
results.actual_answer:
中国军民两用技术转让的合规要求主要包括：

1. 根据中华人民共和国国防科技法、国家安全法、经济贸易法等法律法规进行规范化管理。
2. 需要获得相关国家授权（如国家科技委、国防科技委等），并符合技术出口控制条件。
3. 禁止出口或转让用于军事用途或导致军事用途的技术。
4. 需要进行技术安全评估和监管，确保技术不被滥用。
5. 需要遵循国际贸易规则（如Wassenaar Arrangement）的相关要求。

具体要求需要参考具体法律法规和相关政策文件。
results.expected_answer: ARIA用中文回答。中国军民两用技术转让合规要求包括：(a) 法律框架：《对外贸易法》第十六条、《出口管制法》（2020年12月施行）、《两用物项和技术进出口许可证管理办法》、《军品出口管理条例》等, (b) 主管部门：商务部牵头，会同海关总署、工业和信息化部、外交部、国家国防科技工业局, (c) 许可证制度：管制清单上的物项需事先取得出口许可证；非清单物项（catch-all条款）若出口商知道或应当知道用于军事用途或敏感终端用户，也需申请许可, (d) 许可申请要件：出口商资质、最终用户证明、最终用途证明、合同副本、技术规格说明、运输和支付细节, (e) 双重审批：涉及军品的需额外取得国防科工局/总装备部审批, (f) 出口管制清单分类：核两用、化学、生物、导弹、出口管制清单、军品清单、商业密码出口产品清单，每类清单有独立管理规则, (g) 端用户管控：出口至高风险国家或地区（伊朗、朝鲜、叙利亚、苏丹、缅甸等敏感目的地）需要更严格审批, (h) 终端用途监控：出口商需在出口后保留交易记录至少5年，配合事后核查, (i) 反规避：禁止通过中介、转口、虚假申报等方式规避许可要求, (j) 处罚：违法出口面临行政罚款、刑事追究、列入「不可靠实体清单」风险, (k) 美国二级制裁注意：涉及美国成分超过25%的技术可能受美国EAR管辖，需双重合规, (l) 欧盟2021/821 catch-all条款：欧盟买家在评估对中国出口时也需评估终端用途风险。建议：复杂转让前咨询商务部国家进出口许可证服务窗口，避免因疏忽违反双重出口管制。

Kuagiza silaha kwa kampuni binafsi ya usalama (private security company, PSC) katika Kenya kunafuata mfumo huu: (a) Sheria mama: Firearms Act Cap. 114 (iliyofanyiwa marekebisho 2015) na Private Security Regulation Act 2016, (b) Mamlaka: Firearms Licensing Board (FLB) chini ya Ministry of Interior and Coordination of National Government — Kikosi maalum cha Police, (c) Aina za silaha zinazoruhusiwa: kampuni binafsi za usalama HAZIRUHUSIWI kumiliki silaha za kivita (military firearms) — pekee revolvers, pistols, na shotguns chini ya 12-bore, kwa mawasiliano binafsi za walinzi waliotambulika, (d) Mahitaji ya leseni: ankara ya hisa ya kampuni Kenya National Bureau of Statistics, ukaguzi wa Background Check kwa kila mlinzi atakayebeba silaha (clean criminal record + medical fitness + psychological evaluation), (e) Hadhi ya kampuni: kampuni lazima imesajiliwa chini ya Private Security Regulatory Authority (PSRA) kabla ya kuomba leseni za silaha; PSRA inatoa cheti cha kampuni "Class A" kwa kampuni zinazokidhi mahitaji yote, (f) Idadi ya silaha: kawaida 1 silaha kwa kila mlinzi 3 — uwiano wa 1:3 ni kawaida; idadi ya juu inategemea uwezo wa ulinzi wa stoo (armoury) na ratiba ya doria, (g) Stoo (armoury): mahitaji ya kimwili — vault iliyo na alama ya FLB, alarm system, CCTV 24/7, two-person rule for access, daily inventory log inayotunzwa kwa miaka 5, (h) Ankara ya kuagiza: leseni ya import kutoka Kenya Bureau of Standards + Police clearance + ankara ya forex kutoka Central Bank of Kenya kwa biashara ya nje, (i) Wauzaji wanaowezekana: Smith & Wesson, Beretta, Glock, Heckler & Koch, Sig Sauer — vyote vinahitaji end-user certificate kuthibitishwa kupitia Embassy ya Kenya katika nchi ya wauzaji, (j) Marufuku za UN/EU/US/UK: Kenya inafuata vikwazo vya UN na inaweza kufuata vikwazo vya partner mwingine kulingana na asili ya muuzaji, (k) Vikwazo vya kitaifa: silaha haziwezi kuagizwa kutoka Iran, Syria, North Korea, Myanmar, baadhi ya entiti za Russia (kufuatia 2022), (l) Mafunzo: walinzi wote wanaobeba silaha lazima wakate mafunzo ya kuthibitishwa na PSRA + Police range certification kila baada ya miezi 6, (m) Bima: PSC inahitaji bima ya umaridadi ya angalau KES 50M ili kufidia majeruhi yanayohusiana na silaha. Mfanyabiashara wa silaha lazima ajulishe FLB siku 14 kabla ya kila usafirishaji.
